name: Zoe Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brookside, the Marsh family's farm. They've got twelve thousand free-range laying hens and about two hundred acres of wheat and oilseed rape. I start at seven walking the hen sheds, collecting floor eggs, checking water lines and picking out any dead birds. Then I'm in the packing room most of the morning, feeding eggs onto the grader, which is the machine that sorts them by size.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The hens are better company than people think, and the Marshes pay well because nobody wants to pick up dead birds. The hard part is bird flu. Two winters ago a farm five miles away had to cull all its birds, and every winter since we've had the hens shut in and everyone on edge. I'm still learning to spot a sick bird early, which is the whole job really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold. I'd mention it to Jen in the packing room and that'd be it. I don't really post about things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI was never my worry, bird flu is. If the Marshes lose the flock, there's no work in the sheds for months. I've got savings and the field my uncle left me, so I'd be all right, but I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep on at Brookside and keep saving. I'd do the poultry health course the Marshes keep offering, because spotting sick birds early is what protects the flock. I'd keep renting my uncle's field to the neighbour for grazing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not because of AI. Winter always makes me a bit tense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would actually happen to you if the flock was culled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Marshes would probably keep me on doing the arable side and cleaning out sheds, but on fewer hours. I'd lose maybe a third of my pay for six months. My savings would cover it, but it's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I asked one to help me write the letter to the council about my uncle's field, and it was good. I've never used it for the hens, I'd rather ask the vet.

say: I'd tell Jen in the packing room that AI was **oversold**, and leave it there.
I **don't post** about things like this online.
think: **Bird flu** is my real worry, not AI; a cull means months without shed work.
My savings and **uncle's field** would carry me through a lean spell.
do: Keep working the **hen sheds** and packing room at Brookside and keep saving.
Take the **poultry health course** the Marshes offer to spot sick birds sooner.
feel: **Uneasy**, because every winter makes me tense about the flock.
S0.quote: If the Marshes lose the flock, there's no work in the sheds for months.
fieldNote: Her pre-existing worry is **bird flu**, which could cut her pay by about a third.
She's already a light **AI user**, for letters, but trusts the vet for hens.
The **field from her uncle** gives her a small rental income and a sense of safety.

steps.text: Take the Marshes' poultry health course this winter
Keep working the hen sheds and packing room at Brookside
Keep renting the uncle's field to the neighbour for grazing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to use it where it helps, and farms shouldn't be scared of it. I'd also say the packing room's going to change. I'd say that to Jen and to my sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking side hits the Marshes' office first, the egg orders and the supermarket paperwork. But I think the packing room gets a robot arm sooner than people think, because the grader already does half of it. My job is half packing room, so half my job looks shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mrs Marsh to move me more onto the hen side, which needs a person longer. I'd learn whatever new system they bring into the packing room, once I've seen it work. And I'd put more into savings, maybe two hundred a month more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching the packing room closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think the packing room goes sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grader already sorts eggs by weight and spots cracks with a camera. All Jen and I do is load trays and stack boxes. A robot arm that stacks egg boxes is not science fiction, the big packers have them already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jen do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry for Jen more than for me, because she's in her fifties and only does packing. I'd tell Jen to ask for hen shed hours now, before anyone decides anything. She'd hate the dead birds, though.

say: I'd say farms should use AI **where it helps** and not be scared of it.
I'd warn Jen and my sister that the **packing room** is going to change.
think: The **office** goes first, with egg orders and supermarket paperwork.
A **robot arm** in packing makes half my job shaky, since the grader already does half.
do: Ask Mrs Marsh to move me onto the **hen side**, which needs a person longer.
Learn any **new packing system** once I've seen it work.
feel: **Uneasy**, keeping a close eye on the **packing room**.
S1.quote: A robot arm that stacks egg boxes is not science fiction, the big packers have them already.
fieldNote: She splits her own job in two: **packing** is exposed, the **hen sheds** less so.
Her worry for **Jen**, an older colleague, is stronger than for herself.
She'll adopt new kit **once proven**, which matches her steady style.

steps.text: Ask Mrs Marsh for more hours in the hen sheds
Learn the new packing room system once it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody knows what's going to happen, so let's not pretend. And that people should get ready, sensibly. I'd say that, and then I'd go and do my sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI in 2028 runs the whole Brookside office and probably the egg contracts, so the Marshes save money. But the robots in 2031 can walk the hen sheds too. I'd be thirty-one and my two skills would both be done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd sit down with my savings and my uncle's field and work out what I could do with them. I might put up a small flock of my own on the field, with a farm-gate egg stall, because people still like buying eggs from a person. I'd keep working at Brookside until they let me go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can see what to do, but it's a big bet on not much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is your uncle's field, and what would a flock there cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six acres. A mobile hen house for three hundred birds is about fifteen thousand, plus the birds and fencing. I'd have that in savings, just about, and it'd clear me nothing for the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the robots do that too, eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, for the big farms. But a farm-gate egg stall is about people knowing you. I'm betting there's room for a small one where you can see who you're buying from.

say: I'd say **nobody knows** what will happen, so let's not pretend.
People should **get ready sensibly**, and then I'd go and do my sums.
think: AI in **2028** runs the Brookside office; robots in **2031** walk the hen sheds too.
At thirty-one, both of my **skills** would be done.
do: Put **300 hens** on my uncle's six-acre field with a mobile house.
Spend about **£15,000** of savings and sell eggs at the farm gate.
Keep working at **Brookside** until they let me go.
feel: **Anxious**, because it's a big bet on **not much time**.
S2.quote: A farm-gate egg stall is about people knowing you.
fieldNote: She turns her **uncle's field** from a rent into a business plan.
She bets on **personal trust** surviving where big-farm work doesn't.
She knows the numbers: **£15,000** start-up and no profit in year one.

steps.text: Buy a mobile hen house for 300 birds for the uncle's field
Open a farm-gate egg stall by the field
Keep working at Brookside until the Marshes let staff go

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to plan, so let's plan. I'd say it practically: learn what's useful, save, don't panic. That's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still my job gone in the end, but by 2034 instead of 2031. Five years means I can try the hen idea small first and see if it works. That's a lot better than betting everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a hundred hens on the field next spring, not three hundred, and sell at the farm gate at weekends. I'd use one of the AI apps for the bookkeeping, since that's exactly the kind of thing it's good at. I'd stay at Brookside full-time while I test it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. I'd have a test running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide the hen idea works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling all the eggs every week for a year and covering the feed would tell me the hen idea works. Then I'd grow it. If not, I'd sell the hen house and keep the field rented.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the Marshes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd tell Mrs Marsh straight. She'd probably sell me feed at cost. The Marshes are fair like that.

say: I'd say **five years** is time to plan, so let's plan.
think: My job still goes, but in **2034** instead of 2031.
Five years lets me **test** the hen idea **small** before betting everything.
do: Start **a hundred hens** on the field next spring with weekend gate sales.
Use an AI app for the **bookkeeping** of the egg stall.
Stay at Brookside **full-time** while I test it.
feel: **Anxious** but more in control, with a test running.
S3.quote: Selling all the eggs every week for a year and covering the feed would tell me the hen idea works.
fieldNote: The extra years change the plan from a **big bet** to a small **test**.
She'd use AI where it's **proven useful**, like bookkeeping.
She has a clear **stop rule**: sell the hen house if it doesn't cover feed.

steps.text: Start a hundred hens on the uncle's field next spring
Use an AI app to keep the egg stall's books
Stay full-time at Brookside while testing the egg stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up and people should use it. I'd tell my sister's kids to learn something with people in it. That's about all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is enough for me. I'd be thirty-nine in 2039, with a small egg business running and probably a bit more land. I'd still be sad about the hen sheds, but I'd be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brookside for most of the decade and grow the egg stall slowly. I'd buy a second field if one came up near my uncle's. I'd use the AI tools when they're properly tested, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The world would be changing, but I'd have a plan and time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister's kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my niece and nephew to learn a job where people want a person, like nursing or teaching or running a shop. Not because machines are bad, just because that's where the work will be. They're eight and ten, so they'd ignore me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not getting good at the hens before it ended. I'm only just learning to spot a sick bird across a shed. I'd want to get properly good at that, even if a robot does it later.

say: I'd call **ten years** a fair run-up that people should use.
I'd tell my sister's kids to learn **work with people** in it.
think: By **2039** I'd be thirty-nine with a small **egg business** and more land.
I'd be sad about the **hen sheds**, but I'd be all right.
do: Keep working at Brookside and **grow the egg stall** slowly.
Buy a **second field** if one comes up near my uncle's.
Use **AI tools** only once they're properly tested.
feel: **Uneasy**: the world is changing, but I have a plan and time.

fieldNote: With a decade, her egg idea becomes a **slow-grown business**.
Her regret is not money but **never mastering** the hens.

steps.text: Grow the farm-gate egg stall slowly over the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to bet my savings on the hens in a rush. What would help is a small grant or cheap loan for people starting tiny farm businesses, and some honest advice on what still sells when the big farms are all robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Bird flu, really. Everyone asks about robots and nobody asks about the thing that actually scares me every winter. A robot can't stop a wild duck flying over the hen run.

headlineQuote: A robot can't stop a wild duck flying over the hen run.
portrait: Zoe, 27, works the **hen sheds** and packing room at Brookside, a free-range egg farm.
She is single, has solid savings and a **six-acre field** left by her uncle.
Her steady worry is **bird flu**, which predates AI and shapes even the calm scenario.
She sees the **packing room** as exposed first, then the hen sheds once robots arrive.
Her answer to AGI is a **farm-gate egg stall**, tested small when time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, forcing her to bet her **savings** on hens in a rush.
whatWouldHelp: A **small grant** or cheap loan for tiny farm businesses, plus honest advice on what still sells.
